name: The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England
description: The fiction of the years between Victoria's death and the First World War: the country-house weekend as a model of the whole society, set against the poverty, the suffrage campaign and the imperial anxiety that the house exists to keep out. Its principal novelists are Henry James in his late phase, H. G. Wells, Arnold Bennett, John Galsworthy and E. M. Forster, with Galsworthy's Forsyte saga and Forster's Howards End (1910) as its two summits.
historical_context: The Edwardian settlement was short and uneasy: the Boer War's exposure of imperial weakness, the Tariff Reform controversy, the Liberal welfare reforms of 1906–11, the constitutional crisis of 1909–11 and the Ulster crisis of 1912–14. The 'condition of England' question, inherited from Carlyle and Arnold, was asked again by the new sociology (Booth, Rowntree, Masterman's The Condition of England, 1909).
aesthetic_principles: Social panorama rather than inwardness; the family chronicle and the multi-volume saga; documentary specification of places, incomes and trades; irony as a social instrument; the house, the office and the weekend as structural units; a prose of solid specification inherited from the Victorians and beginning to be impatient with itself.
defining_characteristics: The country-house weekend; the family firm and the professional man; the marriage market and the 'surplus' woman; the city office and the suburb; the imperial adventurer returned; the tramp and the servant as moral witnesses.
historical_significance: It supplied the last confident social panorama in English fiction and the terms against which the modernists defined their formal revolution; Forster's 'only connect' and Galsworthy's Forsyte chronicle remain the period's most widely read achievements.

name: Georgian Poetry and the English Lyric
description: The five Georgian Poetry anthologies edited by Edward Marsh between 1912 and 1922 gave a name to the English lyric of the decade before and during the war: Rupert Brooke, Walter de la Mare, John Drinkwater, Lascelles Abercrombie, W. H. Davies, Edward Thomas, Robert Graves, Siegfried Sassoon and the young D. H. Lawrence. The series is now remembered chiefly for the war poetry it included and for the reaction against it.
historical_context: The anthologies were a commercial and cultural event: cheap, widely reviewed and bought in tens of thousands, they made poetry a visible public property and gave the new poetry of the provinces and the suburbs a platform. The Georgians' celebration of English landscape and rural labour was overtaken by the war and then repudiated by the modernists as tea-shop verse.
aesthetic_principles: The short rhymed lyric; the rural and the domestic subject; conversational ease within traditional metres; the poem of place and of weather; an anti-heroic, un-metropolitan tone; the anthology as the unit of publication.
defining_characteristics: The English countryside and its seasons; rural labour and the smallholder; the village pub and the cottage; love and marriage in the suburbs; the war as it reached the English landscape; mortality and the passing of the rural order.
historical_significance: Georgian Poetry defined the audience for verse in the period and supplied the poetic language against which Imagism and The Waste Land defined themselves; its war poems, especially those of Thomas, Sassoon and Graves, are among the period's permanent achievements.

name: The Irish Literary Revival and the Abbey Theatre
description: The movement founded by Yeats, Lady Gregory, Edward Martyn and George Moore, which built a national theatre in Dublin and a national literature in English. Its institutions were the Irish Literary Theatre (1899), the Abbey Theatre (opened 27 December 1904 with Synge's In the Shadow of the Glen and Yeats's On Baile's Strand), and the periodicals The Shan Van Vocht, The United Irishman and The Irish Review.
historical_context: The revival was a response to the Land War, the fall of Parnell (1891) and the cultural nationalism of the 1890s; it drew on the folklore collecting of Douglas Hyde and Lady Gregory, the Gaelic League (founded 1893), and the patronage of Annie Horniman, who funded the Abbey. Its great crises were the Playboy riots of 1907 and the controversy over O'Casey's The Plough and the Stars in 1926.
aesthetic_principles: The one-act peasant play; the verse play on mythic and heroic subjects; dialect speech transcribed from the western seaboard; the folk tale and the wonder tale; a deliberately anti-realist staging and a mobile, poetic prose; the small theatre and the touring company.
defining_characteristics: The Irish peasant and the land; emigration and the Congested Districts; the mythic hero (Cuchulain, Deirdre, Maeve); the priest and the chapel; the national question and the Rising; the poet's quarrel with the public.
historical_significance: It created the first state-subsidised national theatre in the English-speaking world, gave modern drama its most musical prose, and produced the period's most contentious and most performed plays.

name: Imagism and the Free-Verse Revolution
description: The movement announced by Ezra Pound and Richard Aldington in 1912 and codified by F. S. Flint and Pound in Poetry (1913) with the three principles: direct treatment of the thing, no word that does not contribute to the presentation, and composition in the sequence of the musical phrase rather than the metronome. Its anthology Des Imagistes (1914) gathered Pound, Aldington, H.D., Flint, Amy Lowell, William Carlos Williams, Skipwith Cannell and Allen Upward; Amy Lowell's Some Imagist Poets (1915–17) carried it to America.
historical_context: Imagism grew out of the T. E. Hulme circle at the Poets' Club (1908–09), the translation of Provençal and Chinese poetry, and the example of the French symbolists. It was a movement of small magazines — Poetry, The Egoist, Blast, The Little Review — and of manifestos, and it split in 1914 when Lowell took it over and Pound renamed his own programme Vorticism.
aesthetic_principles: The single image as the unit of the poem; free verse organised by the phrase; the removal of the ornamental adjective and the abstract noun; condensation, ellipsis and juxtaposition; the classical or oriental mask; the short poem printed with white space as meaning.
defining_characteristics: The hard object and the precise perception; the modern city seen as a set of surfaces; desire and the body in a classical frame; the East as a formal model; the refusal of rhetoric, patriotism and moralising.
historical_significance: Imagism taught the century how to write free verse and made the short poem the modernist instrument; H.D.'s Sea Garden (1916) and Pound's Cathay (1915) are its permanent monuments, and its polemic cleared the ground for The Waste Land.

name: Vorticism and the Modernist Little Magazine
description: The London avant-garde movement led by Wyndham Lewis and Pound, named in 1914, whose magazine Blast (two numbers, 1914 and 1915) carried its manifestos and its art. Its painters were Lewis, Edward Wadsworth, Henri Gaudier-Brzeska, Jacob Epstein and C. R. W. Nevinson; its writers Lewis, Pound, Ford Madox Ford and T. E. Hulme.
historical_context: Vorticism was the English answer to Cubism and Futurism, formed in the months before the war and destroyed by it: Gaudier-Brzeska was killed in 1915 and Hulme in 1917. Its magazines and his own novels gave Lewis a platform for the most combative prose of the period, and its typography — the bold manifestos of Blast — became the model for the modernist magazine.
aesthetic_principles: The hard, angular image; the machine as an aesthetic model; manifesto, capital letters and typographic violence; satire and invective; the anti-humanist polemic against sentiment and 'the years of the great English sentimentalists'.
defining_characteristics: The machine and the modern city; the artist against the mass; war as purgation and as waste; the hatred of the genteel and the provincial; energy, violence and the will.
historical_significance: It gave English modernism its most aggressive public voice and its characteristic magazine form, and its manifestos set the terms of the modernist quarrel with the Georgian and the Edwardian inheritance.

name: The Bloomsbury Group and the Novel of Consciousness
description: The circle of writers, painters and economists around Vanessa and Virginia Stephen in Gordon Square, Bloomsbury, from about 1905: Virginia and Leonard Woolf, E. M. Forster, Lytton Strachey, Clive Bell, Roger Fry, Duncan Grant, John Maynard Keynes, Desmond and Molly MacCarthy, and later David Garnett and T. S. Eliot as an associate. Its literary achievements are Woolf's novels and essays, Forster's fiction, Strachey's Eminent Victorians (1918) and the Hogarth Press (founded 1917).
historical_context: Bloomsbury inherited the Cambridge Apostles' ethical seriousness and G. E. Moore's Principia Ethica (1903), with its insistence on the pleasures of human intercourse and the enjoyment of beautiful objects. Its public phases were the Post-Impressionist exhibitions organised by Fry (1910, 1912), the pacifism of the war years, and the Hogarth Press's publication of Freud, of Eliot's Poems (1919) and of the first English edition of The Waste Land (1923).
aesthetic_principles: The novel of consciousness: interior monologue, free indirect style, the lyric 'moment of being'; the biographical essay as a work of art; the informal critical essay; an intimate, ironic, self-deprecating tone; the small press and the hand-printed book.
defining_characteristics: Consciousness and the quality of the moment; the family and the group as a moral world; women's education, work and independence; art and the decorative; pacifism and the state; class and the servant; the passing of the Victorian father.
historical_significance: It invented the English novel of consciousness and the modern biographical essay, made the small press a modernist institution, and gave English modernism its most enduring prose style.

name: The Waste Land Generation and the Mythical Method
description: The cluster of long poems and poetic sequences written in the wake of The Waste Land (1922): Eliot's own 'Gerontion' and 'The Hollow Men', Pound's Hugh Selwyn Mauberley (1920) and the Cantos, Hart Crane's The Bridge (1930), William Carlos Williams's Spring and All (1923) and Paterson (from 1946), and in Britain the sequences of Edith Sitwell and Herbert Read. Eliot's essay 'Ulysses, Order, and Myth' (1923) named the method.
historical_context: The post-war sense of a broken civilisation — the Treaty of Versailles, the collapse of the Austrian and Ottoman empires, the Russian Revolution, the Spanish influenza — produced a poetry of fragments, quotation and allusion rather than of statement. Eliot's notes to The Waste Land made allusion a public technique, and Pound's editing of the manuscript (the 'caesarean operation') became the most famous act of modernist collaboration.
aesthetic_principles: The long poem as collage: abrupt shifts of register, quotation in several languages, mythic parallels, the absence of a single speaker; the fragment as the unit and the note as part of the poem; the objective correlative; a deliberately difficult surface requiring annotation.
defining_characteristics: The waste land and the decline of the West; the modern city as unreal city; fertility, drought and renewal; memory and the failure of memory; sex without love; the dead god and the myth of return.
historical_significance: It made difficulty a modernist value, established the long poem as the period's major form, and fixed the vocabulary — 'the waste land', 'the mythical method', 'the objective correlative' — in which twentieth-century poetry has since been discussed.

name: Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War
description: The poetry and prose written from and about the Western Front: Rupert Brooke's 1914 sonnets, Julian Grenfell, Robert Nichols, Charles Sorley, Siegfried Sassoon, Wilfred Owen, Isaac Rosenberg, Ivor Gurney, Edward Thomas, David Jones, Edmund Blunden, Robert Graves and Herbert Read, with the memoirs and novels that followed — Blunden's Undertones of War (1928), Graves's Good-bye to All That (1929), Sassoon's Sherston trilogy (1928–36), Manning's The Middle Parts of Fortune (1929) and Aldington's Death of a Hero (1929).
historical_context: The war of 1914–18 killed some ten million combatants and about a million Britons; conscription from 1916, the Somme (1916) and Passchendaele (1917) destroyed the volunteer army of 1914. Censorship, the 'war poets' anthologies of the 1930s, and the armistice of 11 November 1918 shaped the memory of the war as a rupture in European civilisation.
aesthetic_principles: The lyric of the trench: colloquial speech, physical detail, irony and understatement; the pararhyme and the deliberate dissonance of Owen; the long memorial prose of the memoir; the documentary letter and the diary; the elegy that refuses consolation.
defining_characteristics: The war and the myth of sacrifice; shell shock and the broken body; mourning and the unquiet dead; the incompetence of the staff and the hatred of the rhetoric; comradeship and the male group; the English landscape remembered from France.
historical_significance: It produced the twentieth century's central images of war and the anti-war poem as a genre, and it permanently changed the relation between English poetry and public rhetoric.

name: Suffrage Drama and the Woman's Theatre
description: The plays, pageants and sketches written for and by the women's suffrage campaign: Elizabeth Robins's Votes for Women (1907), Cicely Hamilton's Diana of Dobson's (1908) and How the Vote Was Won (1909, with Christopher St John), Evelyn Sharp's sketches, Inez Bensusan's management of the Woman's Theatre seasons at the Coronet (1913), and the Actresses' Franchise League's repertory.
historical_context: The Women's Social and Political Union (founded 1903) moved to militancy in 1905; the Times reported the first hunger strike in 1909, and the 'Cat and Mouse Act' of 1913 followed. The theatre was a mass medium and a licensed public meeting: the Actress's Franchise League (1908) put suffrage propaganda on provincial stages, and the Woman's Theatre season of 1913 staged nine new plays.
aesthetic_principles: The short propaganda play and the one-act sketch; the debate play with a woman protagonist; the comic reversal (the men deprived of the vote); the pageant and the mass spectacle; direct address and the aside to the audience.
defining_characteristics: Suffrage, feminism, and the woman's work; the working woman's wage and the sweated trade; marriage as a legal trap; the prison, the hunger strike and the forcible feeding; the solidarities and the divisions of the movement.
historical_significance: It created a political theatre for women before the better-known experiments of the 1920s, gave the movement its most effective propaganda, and produced the first substantial body of feminist drama in English.

name: The Auden Generation and the Thirties Poem
description: The group of poets who came to prominence with Auden's Poems (1930) and The Orators (1932), New Signatures (1932) and New Country (1933): W. H. Auden, Stephen Spender, Cecil Day-Lewis, Louis MacNeice, Rex Warner, Michael Roberts, A. S. J. Tessimond and the young Dylan Thomas, with Christopher Isherwood in prose and Benjamin Britten's settings carrying the group's texts into music.
historical_context: The slump of 1929–33, the means test, the Jarrow March (1936), the rise of Hitler and the Spanish Civil War (1936–39) made politics the subject of poetry. The Group Theatre, the Left Book Club (1936), the documentary film movement and Mass Observation (founded 1937) supplied new institutions; the Nazi-Soviet pact of 1939 and the war dispersed the group.
aesthetic_principles: The clipped, journalistic line; the parable, the ballad and the nursery rhyme turned political; the travel book and the documentary report; the use of contemporary machinery and place-names; a deliberately public, un-lyrical diction; the collective 'we'.
defining_characteristics: Totalitarianism, propaganda, and the political novel; the Depression, unemployment, and the hunger march; class and the English public school; war in Spain and the coming war; love in a time of crisis; the aeroplane and the bomber.
historical_significance: It gave English poetry a public political voice it had not had since the Victorians, invented the documentary book as a literary form, and produced the period's most widely read political poems.

name: The Hungry Thirties and the Documentary Novel
description: The literature of the Depression in Britain and America: in Britain the industrial novels and reportage of Walter Greenwood (Love on the Dole, 1933), Walter Brierley, James Hanley, Lewis Grassic Gibbon and George Orwell (The Road to Wigan Pier, 1937), with Mass Observation's May the Twelfth (1937); in America the proletarian fiction of Jack Conroy, John Steinbeck (The Grapes of Wrath, 1939), Michael Gold (Jews Without Money, 1930) and the Federal Writers' Project state guides.
historical_context: World unemployment reached some thirty million by 1932; in Britain the means test and the special areas, in America the New Deal, the dust bowl and the migrant camps of California. The documentary impulse — the survey, the interview, the photograph book, the sound recording — was the period's characteristic response.
aesthetic_principles: Documentary specification: wages, rents, diets, trades; the collective protagonist and the strike narrative; the plain declarative prose of the report; the interview and the transcribed voice; the road and the journey as structure.
defining_characteristics: The Depression, unemployment, and the hunger march; the closed factory and the derelict town; the migrant and the dust bowl; the means test and the dole; class solidarity and the betrayal of the labour movement.
historical_significance: It made poverty and unemployment the central literary subjects of the decade, created the documentary book as a form, and gave both literatures their most enduring images of the 1930s.

name: The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro
description: The flowering of African American literature, art and music centred on Harlem in the 1920s: Claude McKay, Jean Toomer (Cane, 1923), Langston Hughes, Countee Cullen, Zora Neale Hurston, Nella Larsen, Jessie Fauset, James Weldon Johnson, Alain Locke (The New Negro, 1925), Wallace Thurman, Rudolph Fisher and the magazine Fire!! (1926).
historical_context: The Great Migration brought some 1.5 million African Americans north between 1910 and 1930; the 'New Negro' movement, the NAACP and the Urban League, the Harlem rent parties and the white 'slumming' vogue, the jazz of the Cotton Club and the blues of Bessie Smith formed the context. The movement's institutions were Opportunity, The Crisis, the Harmon Foundation awards and the patronage of Carl Van Vechten and Charlotte Osgood Mason.
aesthetic_principles: The blues and jazz line in verse; the vernacular short story and the transcribed folk tale; the passing narrative and the novel of mixed descent; the manifesto and the anthology; the folk sermon, the work song and the spiritual as literary forms.
defining_characteristics: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; the Great Migration and the northern city; passing, mixture and the colour hierarchy; the folk inheritance of the rural South; jazz, the blues and the pleasure economy; the artist's relation to the race.
historical_significance: It was the first self-conscious African American literary movement, produced the period's most innovative prose in Cane and Their Eyes Were Watching God, and set the terms of African American writing for the rest of the century.

name: The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel
description: The American writers in Paris and on the Riviera in the 1920s, named by Gertrude Stein and popularised by Hemingway's epigraph to The Sun Also Rises (1926): Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Dos Passos, Stein, Djuna Barnes, e e cummings, Robert McAlmon, Kay Boyle, and with them the American editors of the little magazines — Margaret Anderson's The Little Review, Harriet Monroe's Poetry and Scofield Thayer's The Dial.
historical_context: Some 200,000 Americans passed through Paris in the 1920s, drawn by the franc's collapse, Prohibition and the censorship at home; the expatriates produced the decade's defining novels of disillusion and its most experimental prose. The crash of 1929 and the rise of fascism ended the party, and the writers returned to a political America.
aesthetic_principles: The plain, hard, understated sentence; the first-person narrator who does not explain; the scene without commentary; the expatriate topography of cafés, hotels and bars; the collage and the newsreel (Dos Passos); the automatic writing (Stein).
defining_characteristics: Exile, expatriation, and the lost generation; the war's aftermath and the failure of belief; drink, money and the pleasure economy; love without permanence; the American abroad and the American at home; the artist and the market.
historical_significance: It made Paris the capital of American modernism, gave American prose its characteristic modern sentence, and produced the novels by which the 1920s are remembered.

name: The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel
description: The literary awakening of the American South after the First World War: Faulkner, Wolfe, Tate, Ransom and the Agrarians of I'll Take My Stand (1930), Ellen Glasgow, Caroline Gordon, Katherine Anne Porter, Eudora Welty, Robert Penn Warren, Carson McCullers and Tennessee Williams, with the Fugitive magazine (1922–25) as its first organ.
historical_context: The South's defeat, Reconstruction and the loss of the cotton economy, the Great Migration of its black population, and the sudden modernisation of the 1920s produced a literature of memory and of guilt. The Agrarian manifesto of 1930 defended the traditional society of the farm against industrialism; Faulkner's mythical county of Yoknapatawpha (from 1929) gave the region its own imaginative geography.
aesthetic_principles: The Gothic and the grotesque; the long retrospective sentence and the convoluted chronology (Faulkner); the family chronicle and the burying of the dead; the negro dialect and the white liberal's guilt; the local speech transcribed; the oral tale in the front porch tradition.
defining_characteristics: The Southern past and the burden of history; race, the colour line, and the guilt of the owning class; the family and the decaying house; the land and the loss of the old rural order; the violence of the isolated community.
historical_significance: It produced the period's most formally adventurous American fiction and gave a region its own tragic literature; Faulkner's Yoknapatawpha is the period's most complete imaginative world.

name: American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric
description: The American poetic revolution carried by Poetry (Chicago, founded 1912), Others (1915), The Seven Arts and The Dial: the objectivism of William Carlos Williams ('no ideas but in things'), the meditative notation of Wallace Stevens, the plain speech of Robert Frost, the typographic experiment of e e cummings, the long American epic of Hart Crane's The Bridge (1930), and the social documentary of Carl Sandburg.
historical_context: American poetry declared independence from English models in the 1910s: the Armory Show (1913), the Chicago Renaissance, Harriet Monroe's Poetry, the Little Review and the diaspora of American editors in Paris. The Depression and the Second World War turned the 1930s and 1940s toward history and public statement.
aesthetic_principles: The line measured by the breath rather than the metronome; the image and the notation as units; the American spoken idiom; the long unrhymed poem with a variable stanza; the extreme compression of the imagist or the extreme amplitude of the epic.
defining_characteristics: The American place and the American idiom; the object and the thing seen; the imagination's power to hold reality; the machine and the modern city; the American past as a usable epic subject; the poet as witness.
historical_significance: It established a distinctively American poetic idiom and a canon — Frost, Stevens, Williams, Moore, Cummings — that dominated American poetry for the rest of the century.

name: The Golden Age of Detective Fiction
description: The detective novel between the wars, from Agatha Christie's The Mysterious Affair at Styles (1920) to the outbreak of the Second World War: Christie, Dorothy L. Sayers, Margery Allingham, Ngaio Marsh, Anthony Berkeley, R. Austin Freeman, Freeman Wills Crofts, S. S. Van Dine, Ellery Queen and the Detection Club (founded 1930), with G. K. Chesterton's Father Brown stories as its Edwardian prelude.
historical_context: The periodical and the cheap edition made the detective novel the most borrowed form in the new public libraries; the 'rules' of fair play were codified by Van Dine (1928) and Knox (1929) and debated by the Detection Club. The genre's readership included the literary modernists: Eliot, who admired Wilkie Collins, and Auden, who praised the form's pastoral calm.
aesthetic_principles: The puzzle plot with a closed circle of suspects; the clue and the alibi; the detective as a fixed eccentric (Poirot, Wimsey, Marple, Alleyn); the country house or the village as the sealed world; the flat, functional prose that never distracts from the mechanism; the surprise solution as a formal obligation.
defining_characteristics: Murder in the closed community; the country house and the village; the servant and the alibi; money, wills and the family firm; the amateur against the police; the English order restored and the foreigner excluded.
historical_significance: It perfected the formal plot as a literary technology, gave the interwar period its most widely read body of fiction, and created characters — Poirot, Marple, Wimsey — that have outlived their authors.

name: The Ghost Story and the Modern Weird Tale
description: The supernatural short story from the 1890s to the Second World War: M. R. James's four collections (1904–25), Algernon Blackwood, Arthur Machen, Walter de la Mare, E. F. Benson, Oliver Onions, Sheridan Le Fanu's Victorian inheritance, and the American tradition of Ambrose Bierce, Edith Wharton and H. P. Lovecraft, whose essay Supernatural Horror in Literature (1927) supplied the genre's theory.
historical_context: The ghost story was the product of the periodical and the Christmas number, of the Society for Psychical Research (founded 1882) and of a readership that had lost the literal hell but not the fear of the dead. M. R. James's scholarly antiquarianism gave it its most influential modern form and Lovecraft's 'cosmic' tales its American counter-form.
aesthetic_principles: The antiquarian frame and the found document; the restrained narrator and the withheld apparition; the exact topographical and bibliographical detail; the understated climax and the ending that withholds explanation; the short, closed form.
defining_characteristics: The unquiet dead and the violated grave; antiquity and the recovered object; the solitary scholar and the haunted room; the limits of knowledge and the horror of the unknown; the English landscape as a place of buried history.
historical_significance: It is the period's most durable popular form after the detective novel, gave English fiction its finest exercises in the short form, and shaped the modern horror tale.

name: The Celtic Twilight and the Irish Short Story
description: The Irish short story from Yeats's The Celtic Twilight (1893) and the folklore collections of Lady Gregory and Douglas Hyde to the mature stories of James Joyce (Dubliners, 1914), Liam O'Flaherty, Frank O'Connor (Guests of the Nation, 1931), Seán Ó Faoláin, Mary Lavin and Elizabeth Bowen.
historical_context: The short story was the Irish form: the collapse of the big house, the small-town gossip network, the priest-ridden parish and the emigrant ship supplied it with material, and the Irish magazine and the American market with outlets. Joyce's Dubliners made 'epiphany' the form's technical principle and its paralysis the national diagnosis.
aesthetic_principles: The single scene and the withheld revelation; the epiphany and the open ending; the transcribed dialect and the unspoken violence of the small town; the folk tale and the ghost story as inherited forms; compression and the refusal of plot.
defining_characteristics: Ireland, Home Rule, and the national question; the priest and the parish; emigration and the empty townland; the big house and its decline; the family and the repressions of the small community.
historical_significance: It gave the modern short story its most disciplined body of work, made Dubliners the model of the form, and produced a national literature in the smallest of literary units.

name: The Drawing-Room Stage and the Comedy of Manners
description: The English comedy of the interwar theatre: Noël Coward's The Young Idea (1923), Hay Fever (1925), Private Lives (1930) and Design for Living (1933), Somerset Maugham's The Circle (1921), A. A. Milne's Mr Pim Passes By (1919), Frederick Lonsdale, Ben Travers's Aldwych farces, and the revue and the musical comedy of the period.
historical_context: The West End between the wars was a commercial machine of some two hundred theatres and a huge suburban and provincial audience; the cinema, radio and the gramophone competed for it. The drawing-room comedy of manners offered wit, marital infidelity and upper-middle-class leisure as an escape from the Depression, and its best writers made style itself the dramatic action.
aesthetic_principles: The witty exchange and the epigram; the symmetrical three-act construction; the single drawing-room set; the sophisticated, amoral, unillusioned tone; the farce's mechanical plot and the revue's sketch structure.
defining_characteristics: Love, marriage and infidelity among the leisured; the country house weekend; the pursuit of pleasure and the fear of boredom; the changing position of women; class and the nouveaux riches.
historical_significance: It is the period's most performed body of comedy and the last flowering of the English comedy of manners; Coward's dialogue remains the definitive sound of interwar sophistication.

name: The Scientific Romance and the English Utopia
description: The futuristic and evolutionary fiction inherited from H. G. Wells's The Time Machine (1895) and The War of the Worlds (1898): Wells's own utopian and dystopian books (A Modern Utopia, 1905; The Shape of Things to Come, 1933), William Morris's News from Nowhere (1890) as its socialist prelude, and in the next generation Aldous Huxley's Brave New World (1932), Olaf Stapledon's Last and First Men (1930) and Odd John (1935), and David Lindsay's A Voyage to Arcturus (1920).
historical_context: The genre grew from the popular science journalism of the 1890s, the theory of evolution, and the imperial and racial anxieties of the period; after 1918 it absorbed the fear of the machine, of mass society and of biological engineering. The pulp magazine (Amazing Stories from 1926, Astounding from 1930) created the American 'science fiction' out of the English romance.
aesthetic_principles: The voyage and the frame narrative; the future history and the invented chronicle; the evolutionary tableaux and the deep time perspective; the utopian and dystopian inversion; the thought experiment carried to a social conclusion.
defining_characteristics: Science, technology, and the machine age; the future of the species and of the planet; utopia and its cost; the class system projected into the future; the alien and the post-human.
historical_significance: It invented the modern forms of science fiction and the dystopia, and gave the century its most influential warnings about technology and the managed society.

name: The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival
description: The revival of Scottish writing in Scots and in English from Hugh MacDiarmid's Sangschaw (1925) and A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle (1926): MacDiarmid, Lewis Grassic Gibbon (Sunset Song, 1932), Edwin Muir, Neil M. Gunn, Nan Shepherd, Catherine Carswell, Naomi Mitchison, William Soutar and the periodical The Scottish Chapbook (1922–23).
historical_context: The Scottish Literary Renaissance reacted against the 'kailyard' sentimentalism and the 'Clyde side' industrial novel, and against the anglicisation of Scottish letters. Its instruments were the Scots language synthesised from Jamieson's dictionary, the European avant-garde (MacDiarmid's 'Cubist' poetry), and the nationalist movement of the 1930s.
aesthetic_principles: The synthetic Scots lyric; the long meditative poem of national self-examination; the free verse and the ballad in Scots; the agrarian novel of the Mearns (Gibbon's Scots prose); the essay on national identity.
defining_characteristics: Wales, Scotland, and the Celtic periphery; the Scots language and the loss of it; the land and the farming community; Calvinism and the Scottish psyche; the industrial city and the emptied countryside.
historical_significance: It restored a national literature to Scotland and produced two permanent works — A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle and Sunset Song — that stand with the best writing of the period.

name: The American Theatre and the Modern Stage
description: The movement by which the American theatre became a literature: the Provincetown Players and the Washington Square Players from 1915, the Theatre Guild from 1919, and the playwrights who wrote for them - O'Neill, Rice, Anderson, Treadwell, Kingsley, Odets, Sherwood, Barry, Hellman, Saroyan and Wilder. Before 1915 the American stage was a commercial traffic in melodrama, farce and the well-made imported play; after it, American drama had a serious literature, a repertory of tragedy, and its own forms.
historical_context: The little-theatre movement grew out of the pre-war Greenwich Village bohemia and the new stagecraft of Gordon Craig and Adolphe Appia; it was institutionalised by the Theatre Guild and by university drama departments, and in the thirties politicised by the Group Theatre, the Federal Theatre Project and the Living Newspaper. The war years brought the commercial Broadway of Hellman, Wilder, Saroyan and Williams's first plays, and the touring and stock circuits that carried the new drama across the country.
aesthetic_principles: That the stage is a place of literature and not only of amusement; that American speech, American families and American institutions are tragic material; that the realistic room may be broken by mask, chant, direct address and the bare platform; that the playwright is an author with a text, not a supplier of a vehicle.
defining_characteristics: The expressionist and symbolist devices of O'Neill's middle period; the vernacular realism of Rice, Anderson and Odets; the epic narration of Wilder's Stage Manager; the socially documented play of Kingsley and Hellman; the small-theatre and Group Theatre production methods; the Pulitzer Prize for Drama from 1918 as the movement's institutional mark.
historical_significance: The movement created American drama as a national literature: O'Neill received the Nobel Prize in 1936, and the forms invented between 1920 and 1938 - expressionism, the epic narration, the socially documented play - were inherited by Williams, Miller, Albee and Wilson, who made the American theatre one of the great theatres of the second half of the century.
